column6: The commentary says remembrance occurs on the tongue and in the heart; the psalm asks that both its mouth's words and its heart's meditation be acceptable to YHWH, joining voiced utterance and inward devotion.
Hannah speaks in her heart, moves her lips, but has no audible voice; this gives the commentary's inward recitation and remembrance a concrete prayer scene.

column5: Hannah as a model for prayer
column6: The Talmud reads Hannah's moving lips and unheard voice as a rule for prayer: articulate the words without raising the voice, an explicit interpretation of the commentary's inner and audible modes.
The Mishnah disputes whether Shema must be audible to its reciter; this liturgical ruling makes the commentary's distinction between an inward reading and a voiced one consequential.
Moses says the command is near, in Israel's mouth and heart, to be done; the commentary likewise places remembered or recited divine words in both tongue and heart.

Paul quotes Deuteronomy's near word as the message of faith, confessing with the mouth and believing in the heart; this gives the commentary's two modes of receiving sacred speech a Christian interpretive counterpart.
The command's words are to be upon Israel's heart, matching the commentary's claim that remembrance is inward as well as spoken.
Israel is to repeat the words to children and speak them at home, on the road, at lying down and rising; this makes remembered scripture recurrent speech, not only silent possession.
The Torah is not to depart from Joshua's mouth and is to be murmured day and night; this closely joins oral recitation with sustained inward attention, as the commentary does.
The Levites read the Torah from the book and give its sense so the people understand; this is a public, text-in-hand counterpart to the commentary's reading by looking into the text.
The source commentary labels Qur'anic recitation with Arabic q-r-ʾ; here Hebrew q-r-ʾ commands reading the Torah before all Israel, showing the cognate's public scriptural-reading use.

The source commentary labels remembrance with Arabic dh-k-r; the psalm uses the Hebrew cognate for remembering YHWH's name at night, a private act of recollection that sharpens the commentary's tongue-and-heart account.

Jesus promises that the Holy Spirit will teach the disciples and bring to their memory what he said; this parallels the commentary's divine enabling of recitation without forgetting, while giving the promise a different speaker and setting.
After hearing the shepherds' report, Mary keeps and ponders it in her heart; this shows heard speech being retained inwardly, one side of the commentary's oral and internal reading scene.
The message of Christ is to dwell richly among the community, which teaches and sings psalms with gratitude in the heart; this joins remembered sacred words, voiced praise and inward devotion.
The community speaks to one another in psalms and sings to the Lord in its heart; this pairs voiced religious speech with the inward orientation that the commentary assigns to remembrance.

The Hebrew verse assigns hidden things to YHWH and revealed things to Israel and its children; this directly frames the commentary's claim that the Lord knows what is concealed as well as disclosed. WLC numbering is used.
Daniel praises God as the one who reveals deep, hidden things, knows what is in darkness, and has light with him; this closely joins knowing concealment and disclosure, as in the commentary.

In the poem about mining, God-like human searching stops streams and brings hidden things to light; the concrete extraction from earth echoes the commentary's movement from what is covered to what emerges.
Job says God reveals deep things from darkness and brings deep gloom into light; this gives a direct scriptural image for the commentary's concealed becoming manifest.
Wisdom says God witnesses the inmost feelings, observes the heart, and hears the tongue; this closely matches the commentary's pairing of voiced remembrance with what remains inward.
The Spirit of the Lord fills the world and knows what is said; this extends the commentary's claim that speech and its hidden counterpart are known by God.
Wisdom says a jealous ear hears all things and that murmuring does not go unnoticed; this specifically connects quiet, concealed speech with divine knowledge.
Sirach says God searches the abyss and the human heart and sees hidden things; this gives the commentary's divine knowledge of concealed matters a close wisdom-text counterpart.
Sirach adds that no thought escapes God and that he reveals what is hidden; this joins inward thought, concealment and disclosure in the way the commentary does.
The sinner supposes that darkness and walls hide his conduct from notice; this is the mistaken secrecy answered by the commentary's statement that the Lord knows what is hidden.

column5: God's eyes brighter than the sun
column6: Sirach answers that the Lord's eyes are far brighter than the sun and see every human way; the image connects divine knowledge of hidden conduct with the commentary's paradox that excessive light can itself obstruct sight.

YHWH asks whether anyone can hide in a secret place beyond his sight and says he fills heaven and earth; this directly supports the commentary's open/hidden pair as two states within divine knowledge.

column5: secret chamber and claimed divine blindness
column6: The elders act in hidden chambers and say YHWH does not see them; this concrete scene of concealed worship supplies the claim that the commentary's verse rejects by affirming God's knowledge of what is hidden.
Qoheleth says God brings every deed, including every hidden thing, into judgment; this adds an eventual consequence to the commentary's assertion that concealment is no limit on divine knowledge.
The psalm places secret sins in the light of God's presence; it joins what is concealed to disclosure and divine sight, echoing the commentary's open/hidden pairing.
The psalm says YHWH knows the whole word before it reaches the speaker's tongue; this makes divine knowledge of unvoiced as well as spoken content concrete.
The psalm says darkness is not dark to God and night shines like day; this directly answers the commentary's hidden/light contrast without equating darkness with ignorance for God.

Those who fear YHWH speak to one another and meditate on his name; YHWH listens, hears, and a book of remembrance is written. This uniquely joins speech, divine hearing, the name and remembrance as the commentary's scene does.
Paul says the Lord will bring hidden things of darkness to light and disclose the purposes of hearts; this fuses the commentary's concealed matters with its inward remembrance and divine knowing.

Hebrews describes God's word as discerning thoughts and intentions of the heart; this connects recited divine speech to inward content, a specific bridge to the commentary's reading and knowing scenes.
Hebrews says no creature is hidden from God and all lie exposed before him; this is a close formulation of the commentary's claim that the Lord knows what is disclosed and concealed.
The risen Christ says he searches minds and hearts and repays each according to deeds; this gives the commentary's divine knowledge of hidden inward life a Christian apocalyptic counterpart.
Jesus says nothing covered will not be uncovered and nothing hidden will not be known; this closely matches the commentary's movement from concealment to disclosure.

Jesus contrasts what he tells the disciples in darkness and whispers in the ear with what they must proclaim in the light and from rooftops; this specifically joins the commentary's loud and inward/hidden speech.
Jesus says what is covered will be uncovered and what is hidden will be known; this repeats the commentary's open/hidden claim in a warning about hypocrisy.
Jesus says words spoken in private rooms will be proclaimed from rooftops; this is a particularly close speech-level counterpart to the commentary's high voice and hidden utterance.
In the parable discourse, Jesus says what is hidden is meant to be revealed and what is secret to come to light; this parallels the commentary's concealed thing becoming manifest.

column5: hidden revealed in a hearing context
column6: Luke says nothing hidden will remain unrevealed and nothing secret unknown, in a passage that also warns listeners to take care how they hear; this links the commentary's hiddenness with its recitation and listening scene.
Paul says God judges people's secrets through Jesus Christ; this adds judgment to the commentary's claim that hidden matters are known, while locating it in Christian eschatology.

Jesus instructs the disciple to pray in a closed room, assuring that the Father sees in secret; the commentary also affirms divine knowledge of inward prayer, while Jesus makes secrecy a practice rather than merely a known state.

The Mishnah warns that an eye sees, an ear hears, and deeds are recorded; this ethical formulation makes both visible action and audible speech answerable to the all-knowing judge described in the commentary.

Paul interprets Moses' veil as remaining over readers of the old covenant until Christ removes it; this Christian reading makes the commentary's conjunction of recitation, concealment and disclosure a live interpretive question.
Paul says a veil lies over the heart when Moses is read; this explicitly joins textual reading to inward concealment, the two fields the commentary brings together.
Paul says the veil is removed when one turns to the Lord; this gives a Christian interpretive account of concealment as something lifted through turning toward God.

After speaking with Israel, Moses covers his face; the commentary likewise places disclosure beside covering, though Exodus presents a practice of veiling rather than blindness caused by excess light.
Israel sees Moses' face shine and he again covers it; this supplies the concrete pairing of visible radiance and a covering that the commentary's excess-light observation invites readers to notice.
Paul says he could not see because of the glory of the light; this directly matches the commentary's secondary observation that too much light can itself become a veil.

Isaiah depicts Jerusalem speaking low from the ground, with speech whispering from the dust; this is a specific convergence of hushed voice and emergence from a covering/earth, though the prophetic scene is humiliation, not recitation.

The psalm pictures refuge under God's pinions; this is a limited image-parallel to the commentary's hidden feathers beneath the wing's upper feathers, though the psalm speaks of protection rather than feather anatomy.

Jesus' parable turns on a treasure concealed in a field and discovered; this gives a concrete instance of the commentary's secondary sense in which what is hidden can be brought out, without making the parable about divine omniscience.

column5: grass springs in a barren land
column6: God questions Job about satisfying desolate land and causing grass to sprout; this closely matches the commentary's reading of pasture emerging from earth through rain.
The psalm says God prepares rain for the earth and makes grass grow on the mountains; this is a direct creation-motif parallel to the commentary's rain bringing pasture out of soil.
God promises water on thirsty ground and streams on dry land; this supplies the rain/water side of the commentary's emergence scene.
The next verse pictures descendants springing up like grass by streams; this gives the commentary's emerging pasture a close image of growth appearing where water reaches dry land.
The psalm says God makes grass grow for cattle; this is a close claim-level parallel to the commentary's pasture brought forth by the Creator.
The seed sprouts and grows while the sower does not know how; this makes the hidden process behind visible growth explicit, joining the commentary's concealed/emergent pair to its pasture image.
The earth produces first the blade, then the head, then full grain; this is a direct emergence-and-growth sequence beside the commentary's pasture brought out from the ground.

At the meal Jesus gives thanks and commands the bread to be taken in remembrance of him; this is a specific liturgical pairing of remembrance and prayerful thanksgiving alongside the commentary's remembrance of the Lord's name followed by prayer.

column5: remembering the divine name at night
column6: The psalmist remembers YHWH's name at night and keeps his Torah; this is a concrete inward/nighttime counterpart to the commentary's remembrance of the Lord and also illustrates its Arabic-Hebrew cognate link.
The psalm summons all that is within the speaker to bless YHWH's holy name; this closely parallels the commentary's remembrance of the Lord's name with the heart as well as the tongue.

Joel promises deliverance to everyone who calls on YHWH's name; this gives the commentary's remembrance of the Lord's name followed by prayer a specific scriptural invocation formula. WLC numbering is used.
